Precession of the Earth's axis
Investigate the historical problem's Newtonian model of axial precession. Earth is a homogeneous oblate spheroid with equatorial radius Re, polar radius Rp, mean R=(Re+Rp)/2 and small flattening hmax=Re−Rp. Take G=\(6.67\times10^{-11}\) N m²/kg², R=\(6.371\times10^{6}\) m, ME=\(5.972\times10^{24}\) kg, Sun mass MS=\(1.989\times10^{30}\) kg at distance dSE=\(1.496\times10^{11}\) m, Moon mass MM=\(7.348\times10^{22}\) kg at dME=\(3.844\times10^{8}\) m, and tilt α=23.5°. Use one rotation in 24 hours and one year of 365.25 days. After part A use the empirical hmax=21 km irrespective of your estimate. For solar averaging replace the Sun by a uniform circular ring in the ecliptic plane. Set z perpendicular to that plane, with origin at Earth's centre. Near Earth all distances r,|z| are much smaller than the ring radius.

a.1. Flattening dimensions
In \(h_{max}\propto G^{-1}\omega^\beta M_E^\gamma R^\delta\), find β,γ,δ.
a.2. Flattening estimate
Assume the dimensionless factor is one and evaluate hmax.
b.1. Ring field on its axis

Find the direction and leading magnitude of the Sun-ring gravitational field at coordinate z.
b.2. Ring field in its plane
Find the leading field at radial distance r in the ecliptic plane, giving direction and a derivation.
c.1. Mass of one removed cap

Imagine the spheroid as a full sphere of radius Re minus two equal excess polar regions. Find the mass m of one removed region in hmax,ME,Rp.
c.2. Solar torque
The torque on the removed regions equals that on two point masses 2m/5 at the endpoints of the polar diameter. Find the torque magnitude on Earth to first order in hmax/R, and state its sense.
d.1. Solar-only precession period
Derive the precession period T1 in MS,dSE,ω,hmax,R,α.
d.2. Solar-only numerical period
Evaluate T1 in years using hmax=21 km.
e.1. Lunar correction factor
Now approximate the Moon's orbit as a circle in the ecliptic plane. Find T2/T1 after adding its averaged torque.
e.2. Combined numerical period
Evaluate T2 in years.

children.text: Using [G]=L³M^−1T^−2, dimensional balance gives time exponent 2−β=0, mass exponent 1+γ=0 and length exponent δ−3=1. Thus β=2, γ=−1, δ=4.
b.1. Ring field on its axis
The exact potential is \(\Phi(z)=-GM_S/\sqrt{d_{SE}^2+z^2}\). Thus \(g_z=-GM_Sz/(d_{SE}^2+z^2)^{3/2}\simeq-GM_Sz/d_{SE}^3\). It points toward the ecliptic plane for either sign of z.
b.2. Ring field in its plane

Symmetry and the mass-free divergence condition near the centre give \(2g_r/r+\partial_zg_z=0\), so \[g_r=GM_Sr/(2d_{SE}^3),\] radially outwards. Alternatively expand the ring potential through r²: \(\Phi(r)=-GM_S/d_{SE}-GM_Sr^2/(4d_{SE}^3)\), then differentiate. The axial restoring field and in-plane outward field have opposite signs.
c.1. Mass of one removed cap
The spheroid volume is \(4\pi R_e^2R_p/3\). Half the difference from a sphere is \(2\pi R_e^2h_{max}/3\). Multiply by density \(3M_E/(4\pi R_e^2R_p)\) to obtain \(m=M_Eh_{max}/(2R_p)\).

A complete sphere has zero torque, so Earth's torque is opposite that on the removed masses. Both the vertical restoring and radial outward fields contribute. Their combined torque magnitude is \(6GmM_SR^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha/(5d_{SE}^3)\). Substitute m≈MEhmax/(2R): \[|\tau|=\frac{3GM_EM_SR h_{max}}{5d_{SE}^3}\sin\alpha\cos\alpha.\] If the north axis lies in +xz, this torque is along −y, giving retrograde precession.

To leading order the spin angular momentum is \(L=(2/5)M_ER^2\omega\). The magnitude changes slowly compared with direction. Precession gives \(|\dot{\mathbf L}|=\Omega_1L\sin\alpha=|\tau|\). Hence \[T_1=\frac{2\pi}{\Omega_1}=\frac{4\pi d_{SE}^3R\omega}{3GM_Sh_{max}\cos\alpha}.\]
The model gives \(T_1\simeq8.06\times10^4\) years. This is larger than the observed precession period because the Moon has not yet been included.

The same ring calculation applies and torque coefficients add as M/d³. Thus \[\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\frac{M_S/d_{SE}^3}{M_S/d_{SE}^3+M_M/d_{ME}^3}.\] The lunar torque makes precession faster and the period shorter.
The ratio is approximately 0.315. Multiplying the solar-only period gives \(T_2\simeq2.54\times10^4\) years in this homogeneous-Earth, coplanar-circular-orbit model.

children.text: Waves and phase transitions in spin systems
Torque is \(\dot{\mathbf L}=\gamma\mathbf L\times\mathbf B\). Compare with \(\dot{\mathbf L}=\omega_L\hat z\times\mathbf L\), giving \(\omega_L=-\gamma B\).
The equatorial field of ring 1 is \(\mathbf B_1=-\mu_0\boldsymbol\mu_1/(4\pi d^3)\). Thus U=−μ2·B1 gives \(J_0=\mu_0\gamma^2/(4\pi d^3)\), positive.
The terms containing Si are \(-J\mathbf S_i\cdot(\mathbf S_{i-1}+\mathbf S_{i+1})\). Comparing with −γSi·Bi,eff gives \(\mathbf B_{i,eff}=(J/\gamma)(\mathbf S_{i-1}+\mathbf S_{i+1})\).
Apply magnetic torque: \[\frac{d\mathbf S_i}{dt}=J\mathbf S_i\times(\mathbf S_{i-1}+\mathbf S_{i+1}).\] Each spin keeps constant magnitude because its derivative is perpendicular to itself.

Linearization gives \(\dot S_{ix}=JS(2S_{iy}-S_{i-1,y}-S_{i+1,y})\) and \(\dot S_{iy}=-JS(2S_{ix}-S_{i-1,x}-S_{i+1,x})\). Take equal-amplitude quadrature waves Sx=δScos(kai−ωt), Sy=δSsin(kai−ωt). Then \[\omega=2JS[1-\cos(ka)].\] The opposite phase convention can reverse signed frequency. The field checks its positive branch.
\(\omega\simeq JSa^2k^2\). With E=ℏω,p=ℏk, compare E=(JSa²/ℏ)p² with p²/(2meff), giving \(m_{eff}=\hbar/(2JSa^2)\).

The spin wave has no y momentum, so pin cosθin=pout cosθout. Its x momentum is ps=pin sinθin−pout sinθout and energy Es=(pin²−pout²)/(2mn). Thus \[m_{eff}=m_n\frac{\sin^2(\theta_{in}-\theta_{out})}{\cos^2\theta_{out}-\cos^2\theta_{in}}=m_n\frac{\sin(\theta_{in}-\theta_{out})}{\sin(\theta_{in}+\theta_{out})}.\] Choose physical angles giving positive energy loss and mass. If angles are instead measured from the chain, convert them before using this expression.
The ±z states have energies −h and +h. Boltzmann weights give \(p_\uparrow/p_\downarrow=e^{2h/(k_BT)}\). For negative h the labels remain ±z, so up is then anti-aligned with the field.

Normalize the two Boltzmann weights to obtain \(\bar s=p_\uparrow-p_\downarrow=\tanh[h/(k_BT)]\). All curves are odd through the origin. For a large field range they saturate near ±1, for a small range they are nearly linear with slope 1/(kBT), and the intermediate range gives a smooth unsaturated S-shaped curve.
All spins align, with either global sign, so every bond contributes −J̃. For an open chain Eg=−J̃(N−1)≈−J̃N. A periodic chain has exactly N bonds.

The explicitly prescribed replacement gives \(\tilde J_{eff}=\tilde J\bar s\). This matches the official scheme's single-counted energy ansatz. For comparison, a thermodynamically consistent local-field decoupling uses both neighbours, field 2J̃s̄ and an additive correction NJ̃s̄². Those are different approximations, so the next items use the one requested here.

For the source ansatz, \(\bar s=\tanh[\tilde J\bar s/(k_BT)]\). The zero solution always exists. Nonzero roots appear when the right-hand slope at zero exceeds one, giving \(T_c=\tilde J/k_B\). Above Tc only zero exists, below Tc there are also two opposite roots. This is the transition of the stated approximation, not an exact 1D transition.

Expand tanh x≈x−x³/3. The roots are \(\bar s=0\) and \(\bar s\simeq\pm\sqrt{3(T_c-T)/T_c}\). Keeping cubic-order temperature factors gives ±√[3(T/Tc)²(1−T/Tc)]. Draw the full roots from the implicit equation, not the near-critical expansion down to T=0: nonzero branches approach ±1 with zero slope at zero temperature and merge with vertical tangents at Tc. The zero branch persists below Tc but is unstable in the mean-field picture.
c.7. Magnetic phases in the approximation

The approximate model is paramagnetic above Tc and ferromagnetic below Tc, where it supports spontaneous nonzero s̄. The exact infinite one-dimensional short-range chain orders only at zero temperature.

children.text: Use the intercepting disc and the absorbed fraction: \(P_0=(1-a)\pi R_E^2F_s\).
Equate absorbed disc power to emission over 4πRE²: \(T_{g0}=[(1-a)F_s/(4\sigma)]^{1/4}\simeq255\,\mathrm K\), about −18°C.

Let PE be ground emission and PA the emission of each atmospheric face. Surface balance gives PE=PA+tswP0. Top-of-atmosphere balance gives tlwPE+PA=P0. Hence \(T_g=[(1+t_{sw})/(1+t_{lw})]^{1/4}T_{g0}\simeq286\,\mathrm K\), about 13°C.
The relative coordinate has reduced mass μ=mAmB/(mA+mB). Thus \(\omega_d=\sqrt{k(m_A+m_B)/(m_Am_B)}\).

For fixed incoming lab frequency fin, the molecule sees f′≈fin(1+v/c). Thus if fin=f0 the observed shift is +f0v/c, the convention used in the official solution. If f0 instead denotes the molecule's rest-frame absorption resonance, the resonant laboratory incident frequency is \(f=f_0/(1+v/c)\simeq f_0-f_0v/c\), with shift −f0v/c. The source wording mixes these descriptions. Both yield the same symmetric thermal line profile below, so this signed convention item uses self-review.
The Gaussian integral is √(2πkBT/m), so \(C=\sqrt{m/(2\pi k_BT)}\).
Use |v|=c|f−f0|/f0 and the constant Jacobian c/f0. Thus \[p_2(f)\propto\exp\left[-\frac{mc^2(f-f_0)^2}{2k_BT f_0^2}\right].\] If normalized, the prefactor is (c/f0)√[m/(2πkBT)].
The curve is a symmetric Gaussian centred at zero, decaying to zero in both tails. The 1/e points are \(f_*-f_0=\pm f_0\sqrt{2k_BT/(mc^2)}\). The field checks the positive half-width.
Balance upward minus downward pressure forces on area A and height dz against weight ρgA dz. This gives \(dp/dz=-\rho g\).
Adiabatic enthalpy change balances gravitational potential: cp dT+μairg dz=0. Equivalently combine pVγ=constant with hydrostatic equilibrium. Thus \(\Gamma_a=\mu_{air}g/c_p\).

Parcel and environment temperatures become T−Γaδz and T−Γδz. At equal pressure ρ∝1/T, so net buoyancy acceleration is \[\delta\ddot z=\frac gT(\Gamma-\Gamma_a)\delta z.\] Stability requires Γ<Γa, with \(\omega=\sqrt{g(\mu_{air}g/c_p-\Gamma)/T}\). Equality is neutral, while Γ>Γa gives exponential growth. This sign follows the defined positive lapse rate.
For evaporated mass m, ΔS=Lm/T while ΔV≈(m/μw)RT/ps. Thus \(d p_s/dT=\mu_w Lp_s/(RT^2)\).

The water partial pressure is \(p_w\simeq\phi(\mu_{air}/\mu_w)p\), and dry adiabatic ascent gives p=pi(T/Ti)cp/R. Solve \[\phi\frac{\mu_{air}}{\mu_w}p_i(T_l/T_i)^{7/2}=p_{s0}\exp\left[-\frac{\mu_wL}{R}(1/T_l-1/T_i)\right]\] for the first lower-temperature crossing. With Ti=290.15 K the root is Tl≈286.8 K, or 13.7°C. The total-mass definition of φ changes this only slightly beyond the dilute approximation.

Snell gives internal entry α′=arcsin(sinα/n) and internal exit β′=φ−α′. The external exit angle is β=arcsin(nsinβ′). Therefore \[\delta=\alpha+\arcsin\{n\sin[\varphi-\arcsin(\sin\alpha/n)]\}-\varphi.\] A transmitted ray requires the exit sine magnitude no greater than one.

The (α,δ) pairs in degrees are approximately (20,27.5),(25,24.6),(30,23.0),(35,22.2),(40,21.8),(45,22.0),(50,22.5),(55,23.4),(60,24.7),(65,26.5),(70,28.7). Draw a smooth curve with a minimum close to α=41°. Label both axes in degrees.

The random crystal orientations concentrate rays near minimum deviation. Symmetric passage gives \(\delta_{min}=2\arcsin[n\sin(\varphi/2)]-\varphi\simeq21.8^\circ\), the familiar approximately 22° halo.

Mysteries of the Astrophysical Source 3C 273
Part A: Moon's Apparent Motion Against the Background Stars (1.8 points)
The Moon takes 27.3 days to complete 1 orbit of the Earth with respect to the stars, a period known as a
sidereal month. Through a telescope, the moon’s motion is readily apparent, but to the eye, it requires
careful observation over several hours to notice the Moon’s changing position. Remembering that 3600
arceseconds = 60 arcminutes = 1 degree then, through how many degrees, arcminutes, and arcseconds
does the Moon move against the background of stars in
A.1
one hour? One minute? One second?
1.3pt
A.2

Part B: Using Lunar Occultations to Precisely Determine Radio Source Positions: The Case of 3C
273 (1.8 points)
In the late 1950s and early 1960s, radio position measurements with this precision were not available.
While occultations had been used previously, Hazard was specifically interested in their ability to
determine radio positions and structure with arcsecond precision. Such measurements were made in the
optical reference frame thereby allowing reliable optical identifications. Hazard had noted that the
strong Class II radio source 3C 273 would be hiddeb by the Moon (also known as occultation) several
times during 1962 and 1963.
The 1962 August 5 occultation was undertaken at 410 and 136 MHz. Both disappearance and
reappearance were observed and the disappearance record revealed the presence of two components, A
and B, in the source. The disappearance on the right and the reappearance records on the left, at 410
MHz are plotted in Fig. 1.
Fig. 1: The 1962 August 5 disappearance and reappearance records at 410 MHz, taken from Hazard et
al. (1963). Note that time increases from right to left, and that the Moon is also moving from right to
left. The bottom panel shows the positions of source components A and B relative to the limb of the
Moon at disappearance and reappearance.

Part C: The Breakthrough Discovery of 3C 273's True Nature (1.8 points)
In 1962, the year of these observations, Maarten Schmidt was working on the programme of optical
identification and spectroscopy of the optical objects identified with radio sources. Whiteoak mentions
as an afterthought that the ‘current Caltech thinking’ is that the potential 3C 273 identification is with a
star and a strange jet. Given that no other bright star had been proposed as a radio source identification,
he assumed that the bright magnitude 13 ‘star’ (magnitude accounts as a way to measure how bright a
star is; the brighter the star, the smaller the number) was merely a confusing foreground very bright star.
To obtain a spectrum of the faint jet, which he saw as by far the most likely identification, it was
inevitable that the bright confusing star some arcseconds away would spill over into any spectrum of the
jet he would obtain. To offset this, Maarten Schmidt had decided to first obtain a spectrum of this bright
star. On the night of December 29, he managed to obtain a spectrum of the bright ‘star’ which showed
some faint emission lines (Fig. 2), but with no obvious explanation in terms of any expected stellar
lines. Only when Schmidt decided to compare the strange spectrum with the Balmer lines of hydrogen,
things became clear:
Fig. 2: Optical spectrum of 3C 273 (top) together with a comparison laboratory spectrum (bottom).

The moon completes one orbit in about a month, or more quantitatively, moves

degrees/hr. The moon passes through a little more than ½ of a degree in one hour of
time.

Since 1 arcminute = 60 arcseconds, then the moon moves through 33 x 60
arcseconds in a hour = 1978 arcsec per hour of time.

minute of time.

”The ISS loses up to 330 ft ( 100 m) of altitude each day.” [NASA Control Data (2021)].
In 2023 the ISS ﬂies at altitudes of 410 km, with an orbital decay about 70 m every day
(∼2 km per month), and during magnetic storms the daily descent reaches 300 m. The ISS
accomplishes the de-orbit maneuvers by using the propulsion capabilities of the ISS and its
visiting vehicles [International Space Station Transition Report (2022)].
The ISS mass is MS = 4.5×105 kg and overall length is LS = 109 m. Huge solar panels with
a width of WS = 73 m provide the ISS with electrical energy [NASA Oﬃcial Report (2023)].
Including all batteries and other parts, the eﬀective cross area (section) of the station is
approximately S ≈2.5 × 103 m2 [European Space Agency, SDC6-23].
The ISS orbital decay is caused by one or more mechanisms which absorb energy from the
orbital motion, the essential ones being:
- atmospheric drag at orbital altitude is caused by frequent collisions of gas molecules with
the satellite,
- the Ampere force arising from the motion of the conductive apparatus in the Earth’s
magnetic ﬁeld,
- the interaction with the atomic oxygen ions.

D. Drag by atomic oxygen ions
In the thermosphere, under the inﬂuence of ultraviolet and X-ray solar radiation and cosmic
radiation, air ionization occurs (“polar lights”). Unlike O2, N2 does not undergo strong dis-
sociation under the action of solar radiation, therefore, in general, there is much less atomic
nitrogen N in the Earth’s upper atmosphere than atomic oxygen. At altitudes above 250 km,
atomic oxygen O predominates. Layers containing electrons and ions of oxygen atoms appear
on the day side of the atmosphere. In this case, the concentration of atomic oxygen ions reaches
nion ∼10 13 m−3.

E. Drag by the Earth’s magnetic ﬁeld
We consider the inﬂuence on the motion of the satellite of the Earth’s magnetic ﬁeld, the
value of which near the Earth’s surface is equal to (3.5 −6.5) · 10−5T with an average value of
B = 5 · 10−5T.
When a satellite moves at high speed in a magnetic ﬁeld, an inducted electric current
(electro-motive force, EMF) occurs in the current-conducting elements of the satellite’s struc-
ture. This electromotive force causes a redistribution of electric charges in the current-conducting
elements of the satellite structure. An electric ﬁeld appears around the satellite, which aﬀects
on the movement of electrically charged particles in the environment. Electrons are attracted
to those parts of the satellite that have a positive potential (relative to the middle part of the
satellite), and positively charged ions are attracted to those parts of the satellite that have
a negative potential. Electrons and ions that hit the surface of the satellite structures are
combined into neutral oxygen atoms, while the electrons ’travel’ in the satellite’s conductive
structures, creating an electric current. The satellite, moving in space, ’collects’ electrons and
ions from the surrounding space and collides with them. For a rough estimate of the magnitude
of the current that can ﬂow through the conductive structures of the satellite, we will assume
that the collection occurs only from an area equal to the cross-sectional area S of the ISS, and
all ions and electrons participate in the creation of this current.

Theory
Q3-1
English (Official)
Theoretical Problem 3: Cavitation [10.0 points]
Introduction
Cavitation is the phenomenon of vapour bubbles or ``cavities'' occurring in a liquid medium due to drop
in pressure. This is in contrast to boiling, where vapour bubbles are created due to rise in temperature.
Since the vapour bubbles collapse and generate shock waves as well as supersonic jets when the dropped
pressure is restored, cavitation is a constant source of damage and even of catastrophe in hydraulic
machines, ships, and more generally in any device involving liquid flow. On the other hand, it has found
many positive applications, for example in chemical industry, cleaning, and in treatment of kidney stones.
Figure 1. (a) Cavitating propeller (b) Cavitation damage (Source: Wikimedia Commons)
It is understood that cavitation generally grow out of microscopic bubbles, called nuclei, that preexisted in
the liquid. These micro-bubbles are a few microns in size and contain both vapour and non-condensable
gas (the latter is just air when ordinary water is under consideration). If the pressure in the liquid be-
comes sufficiently low, the nuclei grow into a macroscopic size, initiating cavitation. Liquid purified of
such nuclei can even withstand negative pressure without cavitating. One usually compares this with
solid under tension, which does not rupture easily if there are no preexisting pockets or cracks in it.
In this problem, we will be concerned with various idealized scenarios related to cavitation. As is often
the case, we can glean some nontrivial information from simple dimensional analysis. However, we will
need differential equations embodying fundamental laws such as Newton's second law of motion and
Fick's law of diffusion, if we want to conduct a more precise study.
One of the first things we want to know is the so called critical (or threshold) pressure, that is the minimum
value of the water pressure so that the nuclei remain microscopic without growing into macroscopic
bubbles. The critical pressure is roughly equal to the vapour pressure at the given temperature, but the
exact value is slightly lower due to surface tension and the air content of the nucleus.

Theory
Q3-2
English (Official)
Figure 2. (a) Cavitation (down arrow) and boiling (right arrow) on a phase diagram (b) Typical
bubble (see Table 1 for notations)
If the external pressure suddenly drops below the critical pressure of a nucleus, then the nucleus starts
expanding and the expansion rate quickly reaches a stable value. In practice, after the bubble becomes
macroscopic in size, the pressure is typically restored to its original value, and the bubble starts collaps-
ing. We will model this situation by considering a macroscopic bubble in equilibrium, whose external
pressure is then suddenly risen. The collapsing bubble will rebound after reaching a minimum size if
the bubble had air in it. On the other hand, a pure vapour bubble would completely dissolve, with the
shrinkage rate growing unboundedly as the radius of the bubble reaches zero. In reality, towards the
end of the collapse, the bubble would lose its spherical shape, and the compressibility of water would
become important. However, unless a particular question explicitly asserts otherwise, we will neglect
those effects here.
Another interesting question is what happens when sound wave is transmitted through water containing
bubbles. It turns out that not only the bubbles pulsate following the pressure oscillations, but also the
sound wave induces translational motions of the bubbles. These effects can be used to manipulate
bubbles with the help of acoustic waves. For example, in acoustic cavitation, high intensity ultrasound is
employed to generate cavitation or cause collapse of bubbles.
Finally, there is a sort of paradox regarding the existence of nuclei in the first place. The theory predicts
that unless water is saturated with dissolved air, diffusion of air from any nucleus into water through the
gas-water interface must induce a complete dissolution of the nucleus in a matter of seconds. However,
in reality, micron sized nuclei exist in water and it is in fact extremely difficult to get rid of them. We will
consider one of a few potential resolutions of this paradox, namely the suggestion that small crevices
in solid walls or in solid particles carried by water are responsible for acting as micro-pockets of air and
vapour.
Potentially useful information
Vapour pressure
Let us say we have a closed jar containing water and air. If the air is too dry, then its humidity will increase
due to evaporation of water. If the air is too wet, then its humidity will decrease due to condensation. It
turns out that in equilibrium, the partial pressure 𝑝𝑣= 𝑝𝑣(𝑇) of vapour in air is a function of temperature.

Theory
Q3-3
English (Official)
Figure 3. (a) Closed jar containing air and water in equilibrium (b) Diffusion flux through the
surface S is proportional to the concentration gradient across S
Now if a bubble changes its volume in an instant, then the humidity inside the bubble will lose its equi-
librium with the surrounding water, and a new equilibrium must be reached either by condensation or
evaporation. In reality this process is so rapid that we can justifiably assume that equilibrium is main-
tained at all times. Moreover, the heat lost or gained by the surrounding water during this process is
negligible, so that the temperature remains constant. To conclude, we assume that the partial pressure
of vapour contained in a bubble remains equal to 𝑝𝑣at all times.
Henry’s law
While the concept of vapour pressure gives us a good handle on the vapour content of a bubble, Henry
law offers at least a partial handle on the air content. Thinking of a closed jar containing water and air, it
says that in equilibrium, the concentration of dissolved air in water is proportional to the partial pressure
of air above the water:
𝑢= 𝐻𝑞
where, 𝑢is the concentration of air in water, 𝐻is the so called Henry's constant, and 𝑞is the partial
pressure of air adjacent to water. As before, we will assume that equilibrium of air content in the sense
of Henry's law is maintained at least in the immediate vicinity of the bubble at all times, and that this
maintenance does not cause any temperature change.
Fick’s law
To complement Henry's law, we need to know how dissolved air in water moves from places with high
concentration to places with low concentration. This is where Fick's law enters, which states that the
diffusion flux across an area element 𝑆is proportional to how fast the concentration changes along the
direction perpendicular to 𝑆, see Figure 3:

statement.text:
Creaking Door
A block of mass \(m\) is attached to an ideal spring of constant \(k\). The other end is driven right at speed \(u\). Floor friction coefficients satisfy \(\mu_k<\mu_s\). Let \(x\) be spring elongation, \(x_k=\mu_kmg/k\), and \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\). Pure slip has kinetic friction throughout. Stick-slip alternates static and kinetic friction and can create creaking pulses.

a1. Pure-slip period and amplitude
Initially the block slides at speed \(0<v_0<u\) and \(x(0)=x_k\). Find the period and elongation amplitude.
a2. Elongation sketch
Sketch \(x(t)\) for \(0<t<3T_0\).
b. Stick-slip velocity sketch
Now start the block at rest, still with \(x(0)=x_k\). Sketch laboratory velocity \(v(t)\) for three periods, and mark \(v=u\).
c. Mean elongation
For the initial conditions of b, find long-time mean elongation.
d. Stick-slip period
Find the new oscillation period.
e. Critical driving speed
Suppose the oscillation amplitude loses a small fraction \(\eta\ll1\) per pure-slip period through additional spring dissipation. Find the critical speed above which periodic stick-slip is impossible.
f. Hinge torsional stiffness

A door hinge is a thin hollow open-ended cylinder of radius \(r\), height \(h\) and thickness \(\Delta r\ll r\), pressing on its base with the weight of the whole door, mass \(M\). Its upper end turns with the rigid door, while its lower rim sticks. For shear angle \(\alpha\), \(dF=G\alpha\,dS\). Find torsional coefficient \(\kappa=\tau/\theta\). Use \(r=5\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(h=3\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(\Delta r=1\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(G=8\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{Pa}\).
g. Audible door speed
Use \(\mu_s=0.75\), \(\mu_k=0.55\), \(M=30\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\). For slow opening, find the angular speed giving 20 Hz sound pulses. Assume the pure-slip oscillation frequency is much greater than 20 Hz. Give a formula and numerical value.

children.text: Since \(\dot x=u-v\), the moving equation gives \(\ddot x+\omega_0^2(x-x_k)=0\). Thus \[T_0=2\pi\sqrt{m/k},\qquad A=(u-v_0)\sqrt{m/k}.\] The minimum block speed stays positive for the stated initial conditions.
\[x(t)=x_k+\frac{u-v_0}{\omega_0}\sin\omega_0t.\] Draw three sinusoidal periods about positive mean \(x_k\), starting at the mean with positive slope.

The block initially sticks while the elongation increases to \(x_s=\mu_smg/k\). It then slips in a sinusoidal positive hump and returns to zero velocity, followed by another stick interval. The mean velocity is u, so the humps exceed u. Their joins with the zero segments have discontinuous derivative.
In the frame of the driven end, the slip arc and uniform stick segment are symmetric about \(x_k\). Their mean displacement is zero, giving \(\overline x=\mu_kmg/k\).

Put \(q=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{m/k}/u\). The stuck distance in the driven frame is \(2(x_s-x_k)\), so \(t_{stick}=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)mg/(ku)\). The slipping phase misses angle \(2\arctan q\) of a full oscillator cycle. Therefore \[T=2\sqrt{m/k}\,[q+\pi-\arctan q].\]

At high drive speed, stick duration is short and \(\varphi\simeq(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{m/k}/u\). The initial velocity amplitude in the driven frame is \(u/\cos\varphi\). To just avoid returning to zero lab velocity, it must decay to u in a cycle, so \(\eta=1-\cos\varphi\simeq\varphi^2/2\). Hence \[u_c=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{\frac{m}{2k\eta}}.\]

Top displacement is \(r\theta=h\alpha\). Torque on a base element is \(rG\alpha\,dS\), and base area is \(2\pi r\Delta r\). Thus \[\kappa=\frac{2\pi Gr^3\Delta r}{h}.\] The thin-wall estimate is about \(2.09\times10^3\,\mathrm{N\,m/rad}\).

Neglect slip duration. The twist accumulated per stick interval is \(\Delta\theta=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgr/\kappa\). Therefore \[\Omega=f\Delta\theta=\frac{f(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgh}{\pi Gr^2\Delta r}\simeq5.6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad/s}.\] Finite-wall formulas are also defensible since \(\Delta r/r=0.2\) is not extremely small. The field uses the requested thin-wall approximation.

solution.text:
Creaking Door
a1. Pure-slip period and amplitude
Since \(\dot x=u-v\), the moving equation gives \(\ddot x+\omega_0^2(x-x_k)=0\). Thus \[T_0=2\pi\sqrt{m/k},\qquad A=(u-v_0)\sqrt{m/k}.\] The minimum block speed stays positive for the stated initial conditions.
a2. Elongation sketch
\[x(t)=x_k+\frac{u-v_0}{\omega_0}\sin\omega_0t.\] Draw three sinusoidal periods about positive mean \(x_k\), starting at the mean with positive slope.
b. Stick-slip velocity sketch
The block initially sticks while the elongation increases to \(x_s=\mu_smg/k\). It then slips in a sinusoidal positive hump and returns to zero velocity, followed by another stick interval. The mean velocity is u, so the humps exceed u. Their joins with the zero segments have discontinuous derivative.
c. Mean elongation
In the frame of the driven end, the slip arc and uniform stick segment are symmetric about \(x_k\). Their mean displacement is zero, giving \(\overline x=\mu_kmg/k\).
d. Stick-slip period
Put \(q=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{m/k}/u\). The stuck distance in the driven frame is \(2(x_s-x_k)\), so \(t_{stick}=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)mg/(ku)\). The slipping phase misses angle \(2\arctan q\) of a full oscillator cycle. Therefore \[T=2\sqrt{m/k}\,[q+\pi-\arctan q].\]
e. Critical driving speed
At high drive speed, stick duration is short and \(\varphi\simeq(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{m/k}/u\). The initial velocity amplitude in the driven frame is \(u/\cos\varphi\). To just avoid returning to zero lab velocity, it must decay to u in a cycle, so \(\eta=1-\cos\varphi\simeq\varphi^2/2\). Hence \[u_c=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{\frac{m}{2k\eta}}.\]
f. Hinge torsional stiffness
Top displacement is \(r\theta=h\alpha\). Torque on a base element is \(rG\alpha\,dS\), and base area is \(2\pi r\Delta r\). Thus \[\kappa=\frac{2\pi Gr^3\Delta r}{h}.\] The thin-wall estimate is about \(2.09\times10^3\,\mathrm{N\,m/rad}\).
g. Audible door speed
Neglect slip duration. The twist accumulated per stick interval is \(\Delta\theta=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgr/\kappa\). Therefore \[\Omega=f\Delta\theta=\frac{f(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgh}{\pi Gr^2\Delta r}\simeq5.6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad/s}.\] Finite-wall formulas are also defensible since \(\Delta r/r=0.2\) is not extremely small. The field uses the requested thin-wall approximation.

On the circle centred at (xc,0) of radius √(xc²+a²), give the field directions at rightmost R and uppermost P0.
c.3. Air-gap axial field
Using the supplied continuity assumption, state B(x,0) in the gap.
d.1. Dipole force magnitude
Find the x-force magnitude for a silver atom in this axial field.
e.1. Field and gradient at P
Calculate |BP| and |dBP/dx| with the stated geometric and current data.
f.1. Silver magnetic moment
For vz=500 m/s and measured separation Δx=0.20 cm, find μs.
g.1. Velocity-induced spot spread
If beam speed has a 20% spread, estimate the spot-position uncertainty. State how you interpret that percentage.
h.1. Magnetic-moment uncertainty
Estimate the corresponding error bar on μs.

children.text: Equipartition gives mvz²/2=3kBT/2, so vz≈\(5.26\times10^{2}\) m/s.

Transverse acceleration magnitude is μs|Gx|/m. Its deflection during the magnet and subsequent drift is \(\mu_s|G_x|[l_2^2/2+l_2l_3]/(mv_z^2)\). Two opposite moments double this: \[\Delta x=\frac{2\mu_s|G_x|l_2(l_2/2+l_3)}{mv_z^2}.\] The pre-magnet distance l1 has no effect.

Superpose the two wire fields. Let \(D_\pm=x^2+(y\pm a)^2\). Then \[\mathbf B=\frac{\mu I_0a}{\pi D_+D_-}[(x^2-y^2+a^2)\hat x+2xy\hat y].\] This sign matches the stated upper +z and lower −z currents.
c.2. Field direction on a circular boundary

At R, y=0 and B points +x. At P0=(xc,√(xc²+a²)) the x component vanishes and the field points +y for xc>0. More generally on this right-hand circular arc the field is normal to the circle, as its cross product with (x−xc,y) vanishes.
Set y=0 in C1: \(\mathbf B=\mu I_0a\hat x/[\pi(x^2+a^2)]\). The permeability in this model remains μ from the original magnetic circuit.

Differentiate Bx. For x>0 the gradient is negative, \(dB_x/dx=-2\mu I_0ax/[\pi(x^2+a^2)^2]\). The force magnitude is \(2\mu_s\mu I_0a|x|/[\pi(x^2+a^2)^2]\), with opposite signs for opposite moments. The field checks x>0.
e.1. Field and gradient at P
The right intersections are xR=xc+√(xc²+a²) and xQ=xd+√(xd²+a²). Thus xP=(xR+xQ)/2≈0.01624 m. Substitution gives B≈0.160 T and gradient magnitude ≈17.3 T/m. The signed gradient is negative.
Invert B1: \(\mu_s=m\Delta x\,v_z^2/[2|G_x|l_2(l_2/2+l_3)]\). With |Gx|≈17.34 T/m this gives μs≈\(1.04\times10^{-23}\) J/T.

Each spot displacement is xspot=Δx/2=0.10 cm and scales as vz⁻². Linear error propagation gives |δxspot|/xspot=2|δvz|/vz. Interpreting 20% as ±20% gives ±0.04 cm, hence positions from 0.06 to 0.14 cm in magnitude. If 20% is the full speed width, use ±10% and half this spot uncertainty. The source accepts both conventions.

Under the ±20% speed convention the inferred splitting uncertainty is ±40%, so \(\mu_s=(1.04\pm0.42)\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/T}\). The full interval is approximately 0.62 to \(1.46\times10^{-23}\) J/T. A full-width 20% convention gives half that uncertainty. The source omits the factor \(10^{-23}\) in its final line, restored here.

Light drives E=E0cosωt ŷ and cloud displacement y=y0cosωt. Use the negative charge sign in its force. For low-frequency radiation assume ω≪ω0. Mean optical intensity is I=cε0E0²/2. Molecule number density is n0 and scattered power per molecule is s. For numerical estimates take q=e=\(1.602\times10^{-19}\) C,m=me=\(9.109\times10^{-31}\) kg,ε0=\(8.854\times10^{-12}\) SI,c=\(3.0\times10^{8}\) m/s,n0=\(2.54\times10^{25}\) m⁻³,ω0=\(1.25\times10^{16}\) rad/s and ω=\(3.25\times10^{15}\) rad/s. Darjeeling is h=2042 m above sea level. Everest has height H=8848 m,distance d=170 km, and Kanchenjunga has H=8586 m,d=75 km. Earth radius is R=6378 km. Ignore refraction and variation of molecular density with altitude. For the source's intensity comparison use equal effective source luminosities and geometric dilution I∝d⁻², plus exponential atmospheric attenuation. children.text: The restoring acceleration is −ω0²y and the electric force is −qE. Hence \(\ddot y+\omega_0^2y=-(qE_0/m)\cos\omega t\).

Substitute y=y0cosωt to obtain \(y_0=qE_0/[m(\omega^2-\omega_0^2)]\). This signed coefficient is negative below resonance. The nonnegative amplitude is its absolute value. The steady particular solution excludes free oscillations and resonance.

The dipole vector points from negative to positive charge, so \(\mathbf p=-qy\hat y\simeq[q^2E_0/(m\omega_0^2)]\cos\omega t\hat y\). Its oscillation amplitude is q²E0/(mω0²), and its instantaneous magnitude takes the absolute value of the cosine. This distinguishes the signed sinusoid from the nonnegative magnitude.
Inside the uniform cloud the field grows linearly with displacement. Action and reaction give restoring force \(-q^2y/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)\). Therefore \(\omega_0=q/\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_0mr^3}\).
Matching dimensions in s=kp0αωβε0γcδ gives α=2,β=4,γ=−1,δ=−3. Thus \(s=k p_0^2\omega^4/(\epsilon_0c^3)\).
Balance power in a slab of area A and thickness dx: I(x)A−I(x+dx)A=n0sA dx. Hence \(dI/dx=-n_0s\). Since s∝E0²∝I this is dI/dx=−I/L.
Combine B2 with I=cε0E0²/2 to obtain \[L=\frac{6\pi\epsilon_0^2m^2c^4}{n_0q^4}\left(\frac{\omega_0}{\omega}\right)^4,\qquad I(x)=I_0e^{-x/L}.\]
Substitution of the supplied molecular and optical data gives approximately L=130 km. The source uses rounded constants and a ten-percent numerical acceptance range.

Let θ=d/R. In the source projection construction the local horizontal through the observer intersects the mountain radius at radius (R+h)secθ. Similar triangles give \[H^{\prime}=R+h-\frac{(R+h)^2}{R+H}\sec(d/R).\] To leading order in h/R,H/R,d/R, \(H^{\prime}\simeq H-h-d^2/(2R)\). The full source construction gives approximately 6096 m for Kanchenjunga and 4534 m for Everest. Both extend above the local horizontal. Show Earth centre, observer radius, mountain radius and the observer's tangent line.

For equal effective luminosities, \[\frac{I_E}{I_K}=\left(\frac{75}{170}\right)^2e^{-(170-75)/130}\simeq0.093.\] The distances and L must use the same units. This exceeds 0.05, so Everest is visible in this model.
\(L_p=1/(8n\pi r^2)\). Each particle has mass 4πr³ρ/3, so n=ρp/(4πr³ρ/3), giving \(L_p=r\rho/(6\rho_p)\). Convert ρp=\(5\times10^{-9}\) kg/m³ and ρ=3000 kg/m³ to obtain Lp=50 km.

The total attenuation has exponent −d/L−d/Lp. Thus \(I_K/I_{ref}=e^{-75/50}\simeq0.223\), while \(I_E/I_{ref}=0.093e^{-170/50}\simeq0.0031\). Kanchenjunga remains above 5%, while Everest does not. The reference remains the unpolluted Kanchenjunga intensity, rather than being reset after pollution.

a.1. Driven cloud equation
The restoring acceleration is −ω0²y and the electric force is −qE. Hence \(\ddot y+\omega_0^2y=-(qE_0/m)\cos\omega t\).
a.2. Oscillation amplitude
Substitute y=y0cosωt to obtain \(y_0=qE_0/[m(\omega^2-\omega_0^2)]\). This signed coefficient is negative below resonance. The nonnegative amplitude is its absolute value. The steady particular solution excludes free oscillations and resonance.
a.3. Induced dipole
The dipole vector points from negative to positive charge, so \(\mathbf p=-qy\hat y\simeq[q^2E_0/(m\omega_0^2)]\cos\omega t\hat y\). Its oscillation amplitude is q²E0/(mω0²), and its instantaneous magnitude takes the absolute value of the cosine. This distinguishes the signed sinusoid from the nonnegative magnitude.
a.4. Natural frequency
Inside the uniform cloud the field grows linearly with displacement. Action and reaction give restoring force \(-q^2y/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)\). Therefore \(\omega_0=q/\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_0mr^3}\).
b.1. Radiated-power dimensions

b.2. Low-frequency radiated power
Use p0=q²E0/(mω0²): \[s=\frac{q^4E_0^2}{12\pi\epsilon_0m^2c^3}\left(\frac\omega{\omega_0}\right)^4.\]
c.1. Attenuation equation
Balance power in a slab of area A and thickness dx: I(x)A−I(x+dx)A=n0sA dx. Hence \(dI/dx=-n_0s\). Since s∝E0²∝I this is dI/dx=−I/L.
c.2. Attenuation length
Combine B2 with I=cε0E0²/2 to obtain \[L=\frac{6\pi\epsilon_0^2m^2c^4}{n_0q^4}\left(\frac{\omega_0}{\omega}\right)^4,\qquad I(x)=I_0e^{-x/L}.\]
c.3. Molecular attenuation estimate
Substitution of the supplied molecular and optical data gives approximately L=130 km. The source uses rounded constants and a ten-percent numerical acceptance range.
d.1. Visible mountain heights
Let θ=d/R. In the source projection construction the local horizontal through the observer intersects the mountain radius at radius (R+h)secθ. The full source construction gives approximately 6096 m for Kanchenjunga and 4534 m for Everest. Both extend above the local horizontal. e.1. Unpolluted visibility ratio
For equal effective luminosities, \[\frac{I_E}{I_K}=\left(\frac{75}{170}\right)^2e^{-(170-75)/130}\simeq0.093.\] The distances and L must use the same units. This exceeds 0.05, so Everest is visible in this model.

\(L_p=1/(8n\pi r^2)\). Each particle has mass 4πr³ρ/3, so n=ρp/(4πr³ρ/3), giving \(L_p=r\rho/(6\rho_p)\). Convert ρp=\(5\times10^{-9}\) kg/m³ and ρ=3000 kg/m³ to obtain Lp=50 km.

statement.text:
Water-hammer effect
A nonviscous liquid flows one-dimensionally in a rigid pipe of length L and radius R. A reservoir feeds its upstream end B at depth h below the free surface, and a valve at downstream end A opens to atmosphere Pa. Water has reference density ρ0=1000 kg/m³ and bulk modulus B=2.2 GPa, defined for the finite element by \(\Delta P=-B\Delta V/V_0\). Initially flow velocity is v0 in +x with pressure P0. A pressure front moves upstream at positive laboratory speed c. Valve closure changes downstream fluid velocity to v1≤0 in A. The short valve has opening radius r, cone angle β, and a contracted atmospheric jet of radius rc=r√Cc. Its inlet and contracted-jet streamlines are parallel. Contraction data (r/R,Cc at 45°,Cc at 90°) are (0,.746,.611),(.2,.747,.616),(.3,.748,.622),(.4,.749,.631),(1,1,1). For C and D treat c and ρ0 as constants, neglect valve length, use β=90° and use the incompressible steady-valve relation locally. In D additionally approximate reservoir pressure Ph by P0, as requested for the wave-reflection model, without resetting the given initial flow to zero.

a.1. Wave pressure and speed
Find α,β,γ in ΔPs=αρ0c(v1−v0) and c=β+√(γB/ρ0). State the small-flow-speed limit.

At t=0 close the valve instantly. Let τ=2L/c and Ph=P0+ρ0gh. Find pipe pressure and velocity just before t=τ/2 and just before t=τ, explaining the reflected wave.
d.1. Finite-step closure recursion

children.text: In the front frame continuity gives ρ0(c+v0)=ρ1(c+v1). Momentum gives ΔPs=−ρ0(c+v0)(v1−v0). The finite-volume modulus gives ΔPs=B(ρ1−ρ0)/ρ1. Combining yields c+v0=√(B/ρ0). Thus \(\alpha=-(1+v_0/c),\ \beta=-v_0,\ \gamma=1\). For v0≪c, c≈√(B/ρ0) and ΔPs≈−ρ0cΔv. A density-based linearized modulus changes higher-order terms, as discussed in the source.

The acoustic speed relative to water is √(B/ρ0)=1483 m/s, and the upstream laboratory front speed is 1479 m/s. At source precision c≈\(1.5\times10^{3}\) m/s. The pressure rise is v0√(ρ0B)≈5.93 MPa. The field checks the pressure in MPa.

Continuity gives \(v_c=v_{in}R^2/(C_cr^2)\). Bernoulli between the parallel sections gives \[\Delta P_{in}=\frac{\rho_0v_{in}^2}{2}\left[\frac1{C_c^2}\left(\frac Rr\right)^4-1\right].\] This applies for nonzero opening, not at the fully closed limit with zero flow.
At r=R, Cc=1 so inlet and outlet speeds agree and P0=Pa. Bernoulli from the reservoir free surface gives \(v_0=\sqrt{2gh}\).
c.2. First round trip after closure

Just before τ/2 the compression front has nearly reached B, leaving virtually the whole pipe at \(P=P_0+\rho_0cv_0\), v=0. The fixed-pressure reservoir reflects an expansion of amplitude Ph−P1. Just before τ the return front has nearly reached A, leaving \(P=P_h\) and \(v=-v_0+gh/c\). The infinitesimal regions ahead of each front retain the previous state. At the exact closed boundary velocity remains zero until the incoming front reflects, so the stated limits refer to the pipe interior.

After each reservoir reflection, the arriving valve-side velocity is \(v_{n-1}-\Delta P_{n-1}/(\rho_0c)\). The next upstream wave therefore gives \[\frac{\Delta P_n}{\rho_0c}=v_{n-1}-v_n-\frac{\Delta P_{n-1}}{\rho_0c}.\] For n<4 set \(k_n=(R/r_n)^4/C_n^2-1\) and use ΔPn=ρ0knvn²/2. Thus \[\frac{k_n}{2c}v_n^2+v_n+\frac{\Delta P_{n-1}}{\rho_0c}-v_{n-1}=0.\] Choose the nonnegative root. For n=4 use v4=0 directly in the recursion.

Each step line is \(\Delta P=-X+X_{n-1}-\Delta P_{n-1}\). The valve parabola is \(\Delta P=k_nX^2/(2\rho_0c^2)\), with kn≈97.1,318,1646 for the first three openings. solution.text:
Water-hammer effect
a.1. Wave pressure and speed
In the front frame continuity gives ρ0(c+v0)=ρ1(c+v1). Momentum gives ΔPs=−ρ0(c+v0)(v1−v0). The finite-volume modulus gives ΔPs=B(ρ1−ρ0)/ρ1. Combining yields c+v0=√(B/ρ0). Thus \(\alpha=-(1+v_0/c),\ \beta=-v_0,\ \gamma=1\). For v0≪c, c≈√(B/ρ0) and ΔPs≈−ρ0cΔv. A density-based linearized modulus changes higher-order terms, as discussed in the source.
a.2. Sudden-closure magnitude
The acoustic speed relative to water is √(B/ρ0)=1483 m/s, and the upstream laboratory front speed is 1479 m/s. At source precision c≈\(1.5\times10^{3}\) m/s. The pressure rise is v0√(ρ0B)≈5.93 MPa. The field checks the pressure in MPa.
b.1. Valve pressure relation
Continuity gives \(v_c=v_{in}R^2/(C_cr^2)\). Bernoulli between the parallel sections gives \[\Delta P_{in}=\frac{\rho_0v_{in}^2}{2}\left[\frac1{C_c^2}\left(\frac Rr\right)^4-1\right].\] This applies for nonzero opening, not at the fully closed limit with zero flow.
c.1. Fully open initial flow
At r=R, Cc=1 so inlet and outlet speeds agree and P0=Pa. Bernoulli from the reservoir free surface gives \(v_0=\sqrt{2gh}\).
c.2. First round trip after closure
Just before τ/2 the compression front has nearly reached B, leaving virtually the whole pipe at \(P=P_0+\rho_0cv_0\), v=0. The fixed-pressure reservoir reflects an expansion of amplitude Ph−P1. Just before τ the return front has nearly reached A, leaving \(P=P_h\) and \(v=-v_0+gh/c\). The infinitesimal regions ahead of each front retain the previous state. At the exact closed boundary velocity remains zero until the incoming front reflects, so the stated limits refer to the pipe interior.
d.1. Finite-step closure recursion
After each reservoir reflection, the arriving valve-side velocity is \(v_{n-1}-\Delta P_{n-1}/(\rho_0c)\). The next upstream wave therefore gives \[\frac{\Delta P_n}{\rho_0c}=v_{n-1}-v_n-\frac{\Delta P_{n-1}}{\rho_0c}.\] For n<4 set \(k_n=(R/r_n)^4/C_n^2-1\) and use ΔPn=ρ0knvn²/2. Thus \[\frac{k_n}{2c}v_n^2+v_n+\frac{\Delta P_{n-1}}{\rho_0c}-v_{n-1}=0.\] Choose the nonnegative root. For n=4 use v4=0 directly in the recursion.
d.2. Graphical pressure-velocity construction
Each step line is \(\Delta P=-X+X_{n-1}-\Delta P_{n-1}\). The valve parabola is \(\Delta P=k_nX^2/(2\rho_0c^2)\), with kn≈97.1,318,1646 for the first three openings. Starting at (6,0) MPa, intersections are approximately (5.37,0.624), (3.75,0.997), (1.695,1.06) and (0,0.643) MPa. The fourth curve is the vertical line X=0. Slow staged closure keeps these peaks well below the 6 MPa sudden-closure estimate. The source's first graphical table contains a mistyped 5.8 MPa coordinate, corrected by its appendix to 5.37 MPa.

children.text: Ray tracing and generation of entangled light
Eliminate B,H from Maxwell equations. With k·E=0, k²E=ω²μ0εE. Thus \(v_p=\omega/k=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon}\).
E,H,k are mutually orthogonal and E×H points along k. The electric and magnetic energy densities are equal, so u=|S|/vp. Thus Ŝ=k̂ and vr=vp=1/√(μ0ε).

The ordinary mode has D̂=±ŷ, B̂=±(−cosθ,0,sinθ) and n=no. The extraordinary mode has D̂=±(cosθ,0,−sinθ), B̂=±ŷ with correlated signs and \[n(\theta)=\frac{n_on_e}{\sqrt{n_o^2\sin^2\theta+n_e^2\cos^2\theta}}.\] At θ=0 or π both indices equal no. For a genuinely anisotropic crystal these are the optic-axis directions.

The ordinary mode has Ê=±ŷ and α=0. The extraordinary direction is \[\hat E=\pm\frac{(n_e^2\cos\theta,0,-n_o^2\sin\theta)}{\sqrt{n_e^4\cos^2\theta+n_o^4\sin^2\theta}}.\] Comparing slopes of E and D gives \[\tan\alpha=\frac{(n_o^2-n_e^2)\tan\theta}{n_e^2+n_o^2\tan^2\theta}.\] Overall sign of polarization is immaterial.

Let \(\hat t=(\hat k-\cos\theta\hat z)/\sin\theta\). The same two indices apply. Ordinary Ê is ±(k̂×ẑ)/sinθ. Extraordinary Ê is proportional to \(n_e^2\cos\theta\hat t-n_o^2\sin\theta\hat z\), normalized as in B2. At sinθ=0 choose any two transverse orthogonal polarizations, since the modes are degenerate. This vector form avoids the inconsistent expanded z coefficient printed in one source formula.

Ordinary light has αr=0, vr=c/no and Ŝ=k̂. For extraordinary light αr=α, and with \(D=n_e^2\cos^2\theta+n_o^2\sin^2\theta\), \(W=\sqrt{n_e^4\cos^2\theta+n_o^4\sin^2\theta}\), \[\hat S=(n_o^2\sin\theta,0,n_e^2\cos\theta)/W,\qquad v_r=\frac{cW}{n_on_e\sqrt D}=v_p/\cos\alpha_r.\] The extraordinary ray index is \(n_s=\sqrt{n_e^2(\hat S\cdot\hat x)^2+n_o^2(\hat S\cdot\hat z)^2}\). For ordinary light ns=no.

Write s=n sinθ1. Differentiating optical travel time at the interface gives \(s^2=(P_3-P_1\tan\theta_2)^2/(P_1\tan^2\theta_2-2P_3\tan\theta_2+P_2)\). Therefore \[A=P_1(s^2-P_1),\quad\bar B=-2P_3(s^2-P_1),\quad C=P_2s^2-P_3^2.\] Select the root consistent with the unsquared Fermat equation and forward energy flow. At φ=0, \(\tan\theta_2=n_es/[n_o\sqrt{n_o^2-s^2}]\). At φ=π/2, \(\tan\theta_2=n_os/[n_e\sqrt{n_e^2-s^2}]\).

Products of plane-wave phases yield sum and difference components. Matching gives \(\omega=\omega_1\pm\omega_2\), \(\mathbf k=\mathbf k_1\pm\mathbf k_2\), with consistent signs. Multiplication by ℏ gives energy and momentum conservation. Decay of the pump photon uses \(\omega=\omega_1+\omega_2\) and \(\mathbf k=\mathbf k_1+\mathbf k_2\).

The same-polarization channels o→o+o and e→e+e are impossible. Their parent index at the larger frequency exceeds either daughter index, while momentum matching would require a frequency-weighted average of the daughter indices. No cross-polarization channel is universally excluded without additional information relating no and ne.

Put ν=Ω−Ωe, so Ω−Ωo=−ν. The ordinary longitudinal component is \(k_{2z}=K_o-
u/u_o-q^2/(2K_o)\). The source angular approximation gives \(k_{1z}=K_e+
u/u_e+N_eq_{x'}+[N_e\cot	heta-1]q^2/(2K_e)\). Sum these and impose Kp=Ke+Ko. Completing the square gives \[M= rac{K_o(1-N_e\cot	heta)+K_e}{2K_eK_o},\quad N=- rac{N_e}{2M},\quad L=-
u(1/u_o-1/u_e)+ rac{N_e^2}{4M}.\] The centre is qx′=−N. Its tilt magnitude is |N|/Ko and cone half-angle is √(L/M)/Ko, provided L≥0. Signs describe the chosen x′ direction. The source changes coefficient letters mid-derivation and has some dimensional typos in its final angle formula. These expressions follow its stated longitudinal expansion. A general expansion retaining curvature of ne(θ) requires further second angular derivatives.

The joint transmission amplitude is (cosαsinβ+sinαcosβ)/√2. Squaring gives \[P(\alpha,\beta)=P(\alpha_\perp,\beta_\perp)=\tfrac12\sin^2(\alpha+\beta),\] \[P(\alpha,\beta_\perp)=P(\alpha_\perp,\beta)=\tfrac12\cos^2(\alpha+\beta).\] The field checks P(α,β).

The four normalized joint probabilities give \(E=-\cos[2(\alpha+\beta)]\). Therefore S is the indicated absolute-value combination of these cosines with sums of angles. At the specified settings S=2√2>2. The source incorrectly simplifies its own C4 probabilities to a difference of angles in one line, but both the consistent sum convention and a reversed b-axis convention give the same S for these settings. The field checks the numerical S.

children.text: A small spherical permanent magnet can be treated as a point dipole m=q_mδm, represented by south and north magnetic charges −qm,+qm with displacement δm from south to north. The north pole defines its position. A monopole produces \(\mathbf B=\mu_0q_m\hat r/(4\pi r^2)\) and experiences force qmB. Write B=−∇Φ. A uniform conducting film extends infinitely in xy, occupies −d≤z≤0, has conductivity σ, and lies height h below the source, with h≫d. Neglect displacement current and take induced volume current uniform across d. In A a north monopole appears at (0,0,h) at t=0 and remains there. Neglect propagation delay. Initially its image above the film calculation is +qm at (0,0,−h), and below-film calculation uses −qm at the real source position. The supplied film equation is ∂²B′z/∂z²=μ0σ∂B′z/∂t after neglecting lateral derivatives in the thin-film approximation. In B a source moves along +x at fixed h for its whole prior history and is at x=0 now. In C take a type-I superconductor with σ→∞ and a horizontally fixed dipole m x̂ of mass M0 in gravity −g ẑ. Ignore orientation coupling and air damping.

children.text: a.1. Initial field above the film

Sum the real and positive image fields: \[\mathbf B=\frac{\mu_0q_m}{4\pi}\left[\frac{\boldsymbol\rho+(z-h)\hat z}{(\rho^2+(z-h)^2)^{3/2}}+\frac{\boldsymbol\rho+(z+h)\hat z}{(\rho^2+(z+h)^2)^{3/2}}\right].\]
a.2. Initial field below the film
The negative image at the source cancels its field in the lower region, so B=0.

At z=0 the two normal components cancel pointwise, and below the film the field vanishes. The total flux through any patch of either surface is zero. The source writes B′z=0 in one explanation, but it is the total Bz that vanishes, not the image contribution by itself.

Ampère's law across the film gives \(\mathbf j=(\hat z\times\mathbf B_{above})/(\mu_0d)\). Thus \[\mathbf j=\frac{q_m}{2\pi d}\frac{\hat z\times\boldsymbol\rho}{(h^2+\rho^2)^{3/2}}.\] The current is azimuthal and produces the opposing initial normal field.

The induced normal field is even about the midplane, so its derivatives at opposite faces are opposite. Neglect variation of its time derivative across d. Integration gives \(2\partial_zB_z^{\prime}=\mu_0\sigma d\,\partial_tB_z^{\prime}\), or \(\partial_tB_z^{\prime}=v_0\partial_zB_z^{\prime}\), with v0=2/(μ0σd).
The characteristic solution is \(B_z^{\prime}(\rho,z;t)=f(\rho,z+v_0t)\), with f determined by the initial induced field.
The initial image field depends on z+h. Replacing z by z+v0t places the image at zimage=−h−v0t. Thus the downward speed is \(v_0=2/(\mu_0\sigma d)\).
Positive images are at \((-nv\tau,0,-h-nv_0\tau)\). Negative images are at \((-(n+1)v\tau,0,-h-nv_0\tau)\). Their differing lateral positions retain the history of motion.

Put H=z+h. The sum is \[\Phi_+=\frac{\mu_0q_m}{4\pi}\sum_{n\ge0}\left[\frac1{\sqrt{(x+nv\tau)^2+(H+nv_0\tau)^2}}-\frac1{\sqrt{(x+(n+1)v\tau)^2+(H+nv_0\tau)^2}}\right].\] Its continuum limit is \(\mu_0q_mv/(4\pi)\int_0^\infty(x+vt)[(x+vt)^2+(H+v_0t)^2]^{-3/2}dt\). Evaluation gives \[\Phi_+=\frac{\mu_0q_mv}{4\pi(Hv-v_0x)}\left[\frac H{\sqrt{x^2+H^2}}-\frac{v_0}{\sqrt{v^2+v_0^2}}\right].\] At a removable zero of the denominator use the integral or its continuous limit.
b.3. Lift and drag on a vertical dipole

Form the image-dipole potential \(\Phi_T=\delta_m\partial_z\Phi_+\), differentiate for the field, then take the north-minus-south force while holding the image source fixed during field differentiation. This yields \[F_z=\frac{3\mu_0m^2}{32\pi h^4}\left(1-\frac{v_0}{\sqrt{v^2+v_0^2}}\right),\quad F_x=-\frac{v_0}{v}F_z,\quad F_y=0.\] Lift is positive and drag negative for v>0. Both vanish continuously as v tends to zero.

At low v the skin depth exceeds d, so v0(v)=2/(μ0σd), the B4 constant. At high v, δ<d and ω≈v/h, so \[v_0(v)=\frac2{\mu_0\sigma\delta}=\sqrt{\frac{2v}{\mu_0\sigma h}}=\sqrt{v_0dv/h}.\] This is an effective-thickness estimate beyond the uniform-through-thickness low-speed model.
Set δ=d with ω=vc/h: \(v_c=2h/(\mu_0\sigma d^2)=v_0h/d\). For the copper dimensions it is about 54 m/s.

For a perfect diamagnetic plane the horizontal image has the same horizontal moment at z=−h. Its repulsive force is \(F_z=3\mu_0m^2/(64\pi h^4)\). Balance M0g to obtain \[h_0=[3\mu_0m^2/(64\pi M_0g)]^{1/4}.\]
The derivative of the magnetic force at h0 is −4M0g/h0. Thus \(\Omega=\sqrt{4g/h_0}\). This is angular frequency in rad/s.
Use m=(4πR³/3)M and M0=(4πR³/3)ρ0. Then \(h_0=[\mu_0M^2R^3/(16\rho_0g)]^{1/4}\simeq25\,\mathrm{\mu m}\).

Using h0≈25 μm, \(\Omega\simeq1.25\times10^3\,\mathrm{rad/s}\), or f≈200 Hz. The source loosely labels the angular frequency in kHz and substitutes a rounded 30 μm in one line. Angular frequency and cycles per second are distinguished here.

children.text: RF reflectometry for spin readout for silicon quantum computing
Gauss's law on a cylindrical surface gives \(E(r)=\Delta q/(2\pi\epsilon\Delta x\,r)\), radially outward for positive charge.
The core potential is \(\Delta q\ln(b/a)/(2\pi\epsilon\Delta x)\). Hence \(C_x=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(b/a)\).
Between the conductors \(B(r)=\mu I/(2\pi r)\). Integrating flux per unit length gives \(L_x=\mu\ln(b/a)/(2\pi)\).

Appending a short cell with series iωLx dx and shunt iωCx dx must leave the semi-infinite impedance unchanged. To first order this gives Lx−CxZ0²=0. Thus \(Z_0=\ln(b/a)\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}/(2\pi)\). Since √(μ0/ε0)/(2π)=59.96 Ω, \(b/a=\exp[50\sqrt4/59.96]\simeq5.30\).

Replace the plane by opposite charge and opposite return current in an image wire 2d away. To leading order \(C_x=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(2d/a)\), \(L_x=\mu\ln(2d/a)/(2\pi)\). Therefore \[Z_0=\frac{\ln(2d/a)}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac\mu\epsilon}.\]
Voltage continuity gives Vi+Vr=Vt, current continuity gives (Vi−Vr)/Z0=Vt/Z1. Thus \(\Gamma=(Z_1-Z_0)/(Z_1+Z_0)\). The reflected current has the opposite propagation direction.
A π shift means Γ<0, occurring for Z1<Z0. At Z1=Z0 reflection vanishes, so a reflected phase is not defined.
d.1. Quantum-dot potential and addition energy

With electron charge −e, \(\phi_n=V_g-ne/C_g\). Integrate the potential while adding charge −e, or average the initial and final potentials: \[\Delta E_n=-e(\phi_n+\phi_{n+1})/2=\frac{e^2}{C_g}(n+1/2)-eV_g.\] The voltage source's work must be included.

Addition energies are spaced by e²/Cg. As a gate threshold is crossed, N increments and ΔEN resets from approximately zero to approximately e²/Cg. Thus \(E_c=e^2/C_g\), understood as the supremum of this sawtooth if exact degeneracy is assigned to the lower-N state.
Thermal excitations must be much smaller than the addition energy: \(k_BT\ll E_c=e^2/C_g\). Near a particular gate degeneracy the actual ΔEN, rather than its maximum, sets the stricter condition.

\(\tau\sim R_tC_t\). Requiring \(h/(R_tC_t)\ll e^2/C_g\) gives \(R_t\gg hC_g/(e^2C_t)\), which is stronger than h/e² because Cg≫Ct. This uses the specifically requested junction-capacitance time estimate.

Tune the OFF series LC resonance: \(L_0=1/(\omega^2C_0)=6.33\,\mu H\), giving Zoff=0 and Γoff=−1. In the ON state \(Z_{on}=i\omega L_0+[1/R_{on}+i\omega C_0]^{-1}\simeq(158+6.3i)\,\Omega\). Thus Γon≈0.520+0.0145i and ΔΓ≈1.52. The contrast can exceed one because it is a difference of complex amplitudes.

Tune \(\omega_{rf}=1/\sqrt{L_0C_0}\), so the OFF admittance vanishes and Γoff=1. ON impedance is \(Z_{on}=1/(i\omega_{rf}C_q)=-iZ_CC_0/C_q\). Make its magnitude comparable to Z0: \(Z_C\sim Z_0C_q/C_0\). At equality Γon=−i and ΔΓ=√2 in the stated phasor convention.

Add a capacitor Cm in series between the transmission line and the entire parallel LC-dot network. At the same OFF resonance the network remains open, so Γoff=1. ON impedance is \(-i[1/(\omega C_q)+1/(\omega C_m)]\). Set its magnitude to Z0: \[C_m=\frac{C_q}{Z_0\omega C_q-1}\simeq\frac1{Z_0\omega}.\] The assumed inequality ensures Cm>0. Then Γon=−i and ΔΓ=√2. The source's +i uses the opposite phasor sign and does not change the contrast.

children.text: X-ray jets from active galactic nuclei

Use the historical one-dimensional steady jet model. Distance s is measured from the active galactic nucleus (AGN), cross-section A=πr², speed v, Lorentz factor γ, and proper particle density n. Material is injected at rest in the AGN frame at uniform mass rate α per volume. children.text: X-ray jets from active galactic nuclei
Longitudinal lengths contract by 1/γ while particle number and transverse area are invariant. Thus \(n^{\prime}=\gamma n\).
The swept volume per time is Av, so \(F_p=\gamma nAv\).
Injected particle rate is αV/μpp, hence \(\gamma_2n_2A_2v_2-\gamma_1n_1A_1v_1=\alpha V/\mu_{pp}\).

Each particle's model energy transforms by γ, while the number flux has another γ. Thus \(F_E=\gamma^2nAv\epsilon_{av}\). Material injected at rest adds only rest energy, so \(F_E(s_2)-F_E(s_1)=\alpha Vc^2\).
Energy injection is αVc² and rest-mass flux increases by αV. Their contributions cancel in Pj for any segment. Thus \(dP_j/ds=0\).

Rearrange \(P_j=(\gamma-1)\dot Mc^2+(13/4)\gamma^2AvP\): \[\dot M=\frac{P_j-(13/4)\gamma^2AvP}{(\gamma-1)c^2}.\] Substitution gives approximately \(2.8\times10^{19}\) kg/s and \(5.2\times10^{19}\) kg/s at the inlet and outlet. The displayed inputs support only about two significant figures.

The model momentum flux is \(\Pi(s)=F_E(s)v(s)/c^2=[P_j+\dot M(s)c^2]v(s)/c^2\). The net increase is Π2−Π1, approximately \(2.01\times10^{27}\) N with the supplied numerical inputs. The source quotes \(1.9\times10^{27}\) N after rounding. The phrase total momentum flux in this task refers to this difference, not either endpoint alone.

The end forces are P1A1−P2A2. The sloping wall contributes an outward axial component, giving \[F_{Pr}=P_1A_1-P_2A_2+\int_{r_1}^{r_2}2\pi rP[s(r)]\,dr,\quad s(r)=s_1+\frac{s_2-s_1}{r_2-r_1}(r-r_1).\] The integral is about \(9.71\times10^{26}\) N and the net force about \(8.10\times10^{26}\) N with the supplied inputs. The source rounds these to \(9.8\times10^{26}\) N and \(8.2\times10^{26}\) N.

The model would require Π=FPr. With the quoted rounded results, \(|1.9-0.82|/0.82\times100\%\simeq132\%\). Direct calculation before rounding gives about 148% from Π≈\(2.01\times10^{27}\) N and FPr≈\(8.10\times10^{26}\) N. The source prints 40%, inconsistent with both its stated denominator and its displayed numbers. Use the defined denominator and show your arithmetic.
\[u=U/V=\int_0^\infty\epsilon f(\epsilon)\,d\epsilon.\] Physical distributions must have cutoffs or decay sufficiently rapidly for this integral to exist.

A particle incident at θ carries normal momentum (ε/c)cosθ and reverses it. The incident flux includes c cosθ and solid-angle weight sinθ dθdφ/(4π). Integrating the incident hemisphere gives \[\frac{\Delta p_z}{\Delta t}=\frac{\Delta A}{3}\int_0^\infty\epsilon f(\epsilon)d\epsilon.\] The gas momentum change is opposite to the force on the wall.
Divide the wall force by area to obtain P=u/3, or \(U=3PV\).
With no heat input, dU=−P dV. Since U=3PV, \(3VdP+4PdV=0\). Integrate to get \(PV^{4/3}=\text{constant}\).

The perpendicular speed is v sinφ. Force balance is \(eBv\sin\phi=\gamma m\Omega_gv\sin\phi\), giving \(\Omega_g=eB/(\gamma m)\), independent of nonzero pitch. The speed of the unit velocity vector on the direction sphere is \(\Omega_g\sin\phi\). The source calls the latter Ω but labels it gyration frequency. The distinction is needed to retain the correct pitch dependence.

The emission direction traverses an angular width 2/γ at rate Ωg sinφ, so emission duration is \(2/(\gamma\Omega_g\sin\phi)\). Arrival-time compression is of order 1−v/c≈1/(2γ²). Thus \[\Delta t_{obs}\sim\frac{m}{\gamma^2eB\sin\phi}.\] Numerical cone factors are approximate. The source's pitch-independent result corresponds to sinφ≈1 and should not be applied at arbitrary pitch.

\[\nu_{chr}\sim1/\Delta t_{obs}\sim\gamma^2eB\sin\phi/m.\] This is a characteristic inverse width, not the gyrofrequency in cycles per second. A precise spectral-peak calculation supplies additional numerical factors.
\(\tau=E/P_s=6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5/[e^4B^2E\sin^2\phi]\). It is an instantaneous loss timescale, decreasing with energy.

Linear dimensions scale as (V/V0)^(1/3), and any material area as (V/V0)^(2/3). Conserved flux gives \(B=B_0(V/V_0)^{-2/3}\). The relevant flux is through a material cross-section, not the identically zero net flux through a closed surface.

Let a=V/V0. From U∝V^(−1/3), each energy scales as ε=ε0 a^(−1/3). Conservation in an energy bin gives \(Vf(\epsilon)d\epsilon=V_0f_0(\epsilon_0)d\epsilon_0\). Therefore \[f(\epsilon)=\kappa_0a^{-(p+2)/3}\epsilon^{-p}.\] The energy bounds scale by a^(−1/3). The source's a^−1 normalization omits the energy-bin Jacobian and energy shift, and integrates an unbounded power law that need not converge. The slope stays p but its normalization is not simple number dilution.

For fixed field and pitch, \(\dot\epsilon=-a_s\epsilon^2\), so \(\epsilon(t)=\epsilon_i/(1+a_s\epsilon_it)\) and loss time is 1/(as εi). Higher energies cool faster. An initially finite power-law population develops a high-energy cutoff or break rather than preserving its original spectrum. For an impulsive population, \(f(\epsilon,t)=\kappa\epsilon^{-p}(1-a_st\epsilon)^{p-2}\) below the evolving cutoff, so p>2 gives progressive high-energy suppression. A universal slope increase for every p or injection history cannot be inferred from the loss law alone.

Adiabatic expansion preserves the power-law slope while reducing field and density, favouring it for AX1C and BX2. Synchrotron cooling preferentially affects the highest-energy electrons and their X-rays, favouring it for HST-1 and Knot A because their lower-frequency brightness is unchanged. These are comparative interpretations within the two mechanisms posed, not unique exclusions of all possible astrophysical causes.

children.text: \[\mathbf F_{ext}=(N-mg)\hat z+\mathbf F_f.\] Weight acts at C downward, N acts at A upward, and tangential friction acts at A opposite vA. The xy sketch must show opposite vA and Ff arrows. No absolute horizontal direction is prescribed.
a.2. Torque about centre of mass

Gravity has no torque about C. The contact torque is \(\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf a\times(N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\), or \[\tau_x=R(1-\alpha\cos\theta)F_{f,y},\quad\tau_y=R(\alpha\cos\theta-1)F_{f,x}-\alpha RN\sin\theta,\quad\tau_z=\alpha R\sin\theta F_{f,y}.\]

The material velocity at contact is \(\mathbf v_A=\dot{\mathbf s}+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf a\). Although a labels the instantaneous geometric contact rather than one fixed material point, \(\dot{\mathbf a}=\alpha R\dot{\hat3}\) and \(\dot{\hat3}=\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3\). The difference between adot and ω×a is horizontal. Therefore \(\mathbf v_A\cdot\hat z=(\dot{\mathbf s}+\dot{\mathbf a})\cdot\hat z=d[(\mathbf s+\mathbf a)\cdot\hat z]/dt=0\).
a.4. Angular velocity in both frames

Add the precession, tilt and spin: \(\boldsymbol\omega=\dot\phi\hat z+\dot\theta\hat2+\dot\psi\hat3\). Thus \[\boldsymbol\omega=\dot\psi\sin\theta\hat x+\dot\theta\hat y+(\dot\phi+\dot\psi\cos\theta)\hat z\] and \[\boldsymbol\omega=-\dot\phi\sin\theta\hat1+\dot\theta\hat2+(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)\hat3.\]

\(U_g=mgR(1-\alpha\cos\theta)\), \(K_R=[I_1(\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta)+I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)^2]/2\). The centre velocity is \[\dot{\mathbf s}=[v_x+R\dot\theta(1-\alpha\cos\theta)]\hat x+[v_y-R\sin\theta(\alpha\dot\phi+\dot\psi)]\hat y+\alpha R\dot\theta\sin\theta\hat z.\] Hence KT=m|sdot|²/2 and ET=KT+KR+Ug. Squaring the displayed components gives the requested explicit expression.
The z axis is fixed in inertial space, so \(\dot L_z=\tau_z=\alpha R\sin\theta F_{f,y}\).

Contact-force power splits into centre work \((N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\cdot\dot{\mathbf s}\) and torque power \(\boldsymbol\tau\cdot\boldsymbol\omega\). Their sum is contact power \((N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\cdot\mathbf v_A\). Since vAz=0, \[\dot E_T=\mathbf F_f\cdot\mathbf v_A=-\mu_kN|\mathbf v_A|\le0.\] Gravity exchanges kinetic and potential energy, with \(\dot U_g=mg\alpha R\sin\theta\dot\theta\). The normal force can do centre-of-mass work but has zero total rigid-body power at contact. Frictional Fy and its x,z torque components change vertical angular momentum and facilitate spin-to-tilt energy transfer. Friction dissipates total energy while rotational energy supplies the gravitational rise.

ET decreases under sliding friction and approaches the final gravitational energy at rest. Ug rises during inversion and becomes constant when the stem-supported height settles. KT starts near zero, rises transiently and returns near zero in phase IV and to zero in V. KR is initially dominant, decreases overall as energy is transferred and dissipated, and vanishes in V. The source sketches it monotonically falling as a qualitative typical history, rather than a theorem for every possible trajectory. Draw all components consistently with ET=Ug+KT+KR. The spherical-contact formula for Ug ceases to apply once support transfers to the stem.
Axisymmetry gives \(\mathbf L=I_1\boldsymbol\omega+(I_3-I_1)(\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\hat3)\hat3\). Cross with 3hat: the second term vanishes and k=I1.

Choose \(\mathbf v=\mathbf a=\alpha R\hat3-R\hat z\), or its negative, which changes only the convention for λ. Then \[\dot\lambda=\dot{\mathbf L}\cdot\mathbf a+\alpha R\mathbf L\cdot(\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3).\] The first term vanishes because contact torque is a×F. By A9, \(\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3=(\mathbf L\times\hat3)/I_1\), so the second term also vanishes. It is essential to differentiate the moving vector a: torque perpendicular to a alone would not prove conservation.

solution.text:
Tippe top
a.1. Force diagram
\[\mathbf F_{ext}=(N-mg)\hat z+\mathbf F_f.\] Weight acts at C downward, N acts at A upward, and tangential friction acts at A opposite vA. The xy sketch must show opposite vA and Ff arrows. No absolute horizontal direction is prescribed.
a.2. Torque about centre of mass
Gravity has no torque about C. The contact torque is \(\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf a\times(N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\), or \[\tau_x=R(1-\alpha\cos\theta)F_{f,y},\quad\tau_y=R(\alpha\cos\theta-1)F_{f,x}-\alpha RN\sin\theta,\quad\tau_z=\alpha R\sin\theta F_{f,y}.\]
a.3. No vertical contact velocity
The material velocity at contact is \(\mathbf v_A=\dot{\mathbf s}+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf a\). Although a labels the instantaneous geometric contact rather than one fixed material point, \(\dot{\mathbf a}=\alpha R\dot{\hat3}\) and \(\dot{\hat3}=\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3\). The difference between adot and ω×a is horizontal. Therefore \(\mathbf v_A\cdot\hat z=(\dot{\mathbf s}+\dot{\mathbf a})\cdot\hat z=d[(\mathbf s+\mathbf a)\cdot\hat z]/dt=0\).
a.4. Angular velocity in both frames
Add the precession, tilt and spin: \(\boldsymbol\omega=\dot\phi\hat z+\dot\theta\hat2+\dot\psi\hat3\). Thus \[\boldsymbol\omega=\dot\psi\sin\theta\hat x+\dot\theta\hat y+(\dot\phi+\dot\psi\cos\theta)\hat z\] and \[\boldsymbol\omega=-\dot\phi\sin\theta\hat1+\dot\theta\hat2+(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)\hat3.\]
a.5. Energy in contact variables
\(U_g=mgR(1-\alpha\cos\theta)\), \(K_R=[I_1(\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta)+I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)^2]/2\). The centre velocity is \[\dot{\mathbf s}=[v_x+R\dot\theta(1-\alpha\cos\theta)]\hat x+[v_y-R\sin\theta(\alpha\dot\phi+\dot\psi)]\hat y+\alpha R\dot\theta\sin\theta\hat z.\] Hence KT=m|sdot|²/2 and ET=KT+KR+Ug. Squaring the displayed components gives the requested explicit expression.
a.6. Vertical angular momentum rate
The z axis is fixed in inertial space, so \(\dot L_z=\tau_z=\alpha R\sin\theta F_{f,y}\).
a.7. Energy transfer and dissipation
Contact-force power splits into centre work \((N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\cdot\dot{\mathbf s}\) and torque power \(\boldsymbol\tau\cdot\boldsymbol\omega\). Their sum is contact power \((N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\cdot\mathbf v_A\). Since vAz=0, \[\dot E_T=\mathbf F_f\cdot\mathbf v_A=-\mu_kN|\mathbf v_A|\le0.\] Gravity exchanges kinetic and potential energy, with \(\dot U_g=mg\alpha R\sin\theta\dot\theta\). The normal force can do centre-of-mass work but has zero total rigid-body power at contact. Frictional Fy and its x,z torque components change vertical angular momentum and facilitate spin-to-tilt energy transfer. Friction dissipates total energy while rotational energy supplies the gravitational rise.
a.8. Energy sketches through inversion
ET decreases under sliding friction and approaches the final gravitational energy at rest. Ug rises during inversion and becomes constant when the stem-supported height settles. KT starts near zero, rises transiently and returns near zero in phase IV and to zero in V. KR is initially dominant, decreases overall as energy is transferred and dissipated, and vanishes in V. The source sketches it monotonically falling as a qualitative typical history, rather than a theorem for every possible trajectory. Draw all components consistently with ET=Ug+KT+KR. The spherical-contact formula for Ug ceases to apply once support transfers to the stem.
a.9. Transverse inertia identity
Axisymmetry gives \(\mathbf L=I_1\boldsymbol\omega+(I_3-I_1)(\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\hat3)\hat3\). Cross with 3hat: the second term vanishes and k=I1.
a.10. Jellett integral
Choose \(\mathbf v=\mathbf a=\alpha R\hat3-R\hat z\), or its negative, which changes only the convention for λ. Then \[\dot\lambda=\dot{\mathbf L}\cdot\mathbf a+\alpha R\mathbf L\cdot(\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3).\] The first term vanishes because contact torque is a×F. By A9, \(\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3=(\mathbf L\times\hat3)/I_1\), so the second term also vanishes. It is essential to differentiate the moving vector a: torque perpendicular to a alone would not prove conservation.

children.text: The two charge forces do total work \(dW=\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf p\), giving \(P_{abs}=\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf p}\).

For p=αE, \(W=\int_0^{E_0}E\alpha dE=\alpha E_0^2/2=\mathbf p_0\cdot\mathbf E_0/2\). The induced mechanical trapping potential is \(U_{ind}=-\mathbf p_0\cdot\mathbf E_0/2\). The factor one half accounts for inducing the dipole.
\(\langle\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf p}\rangle=-\alpha\omega E_0^2\sin\phi/2\). Thus \[\Gamma_{sc}=-\frac{\alpha I\sin\phi}{\hbar\epsilon_0c}.\] With the lag convention sinφ≤0, this is nonnegative.

Put \(D=\sqrt{(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma_\omega^2\omega^2}\). Then \[\alpha=\frac{e^2}{m_eD},\quad\cos\phi=\frac{\omega_0^2-\omega^2}{D},\quad\sin\phi=-\frac{\gamma_\omega\omega}{D}.\] The source instead permits a negative α and shifts φ by π. The observable products αcosφ and αsinφ agree.

The ratio is \(\tfrac12\cot\phi=-(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)/(2\gamma_\omega\omega)\). With \(\gamma_\omega=\gamma(\omega/\omega_0)^2\), \[\frac{U_{dip}}{\hbar\Gamma_{sc}}=-\frac{\omega_0^2(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}{2\gamma\omega^3}.\] It is negative for red detuning ω<ω0.
The deepest point is ρ=z=0. Replace e²/(ε0me) by 6πc³γ/ω0² to obtain \[U_{depth}=\frac{6c^2\gamma P(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}{\omega_0^2D_0^2[(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^6/\omega_0^4]}.\]

\(\omega=2\pi c/\lambda\), \(\omega_0=2\pi c/\lambda_0\), γ≈\(6.4\times10^{7}\) s^−1. These give Udepth/kB≈4.13 μK. The source also accepts thermal-energy conventions f kBT0, with f=1/2 or 3/2, but this field fixes f=1.

Using the source's estimate pz0≈ħ gives \(E-U_{min}\sim m\Omega_z^2z_0^2/2+\hbar^2/(2mz_0^2)\), minimized at \(z_0\sim\sqrt{\hbar/(m\Omega_z)}\). If z0 means exact rms width, use Δz=√[ħ/(2mΩz)]. Numerical width factors depend on this choice.

The source's pz0≈ħ estimate yields \(E_{min}-U_{min}\sim\hbar\Omega_z\). The exact quantum harmonic oscillator gives \(E_{min}-U_{min}=\hbar\Omega_z/2\). Both convey the requested scale and the source accepts the exact result.
The uncertainty estimate gives \(v_z\sim\hbar/(mz_0)\sim\sqrt{\hbar\Omega_z/m}\). This is a typical or rms scale, not signed mean velocity, which vanishes. The exact rms speed is √[ħΩz/(2m)].

For per-axis widths, \(x_0/z_0=\sqrt{\Omega_z/\Omega_\rho}\). If \(\rho_0=\sqrt{x_0^2+y_0^2}\), then \(\rho_0/z_0=\sqrt{2\Omega_z/\Omega_\rho}\). The initially tighter radial confinement makes a cigar-shaped cloud. The source accepts either explicit width convention.
For one transverse component, \(v_x/v_z=\sqrt{\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). For combined radial rms speed, \(v_\rho/v_z=\sqrt{2\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). Confinement and velocity width vary oppositely.

The late width ratio is the velocity ratio. Per-axis \(x_L/z_L\to\sqrt{\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\), or combined radial \(\rho_L/z_L\to\sqrt{2\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). The condensate expands faster in the initially tightly confined direction, reversing the visible anisotropy.

Maxwell velocities have equal Cartesian rms components. Thus late per-axis widths satisfy xL/zL=1 and the cloud is spherical, unlike the condensate. A combined radial rms width √〈x²+y²〉 divided by axial rms width is √2 even for a sphere. This geometric convention must not be confused with visible anisotropy. The source's quoted ratio 1 refers to equal widths along individual directions.

3.2. Equal-end-area tower radius
If the upper and lower end cross-sections are equal, find the top radius from Earth centre.
3.3. Taper ratio
Find \(A_G/A_S\) for nanotube strength 130 GPa and density \(1300\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\).
3.4. Counterweight relation
Terminate the tower with a counterweight of mass \(m_C\) at height \(h_C\) above geostationary radius. Find its mass in terms of \(h_C\) and the tapered-tower parameters.
4.1. Earth escape release radius
Find the radius at which a payload released from rest relative to the tower can escape Earth.
4.2. Solar distance extrema
The tower top is 107000 km from Earth centre. Assume tower motion is in Earth's orbital plane and neglect Earth gravity at release. Find the minimum and maximum solar distances attainable by releasing a payload from rest relative to the tower, in AU.

children.text: Radial force balance gives \(d\sigma/dr=\rho GM(1/r^2-r/R_G^3)\). Integrate from R, where stress is zero. Setting it to zero again at top radius H gives \(RH^2+R^2H-2R_G^3=0\), after discarding the trivial zero-length root. Thus \[H=\frac R2\left[\sqrt{1+8(R_G/R)^3}-1\right],\qquad h_{top}=H-R\simeq1.45\times10^5\,\mathrm{km}.\]
The derivative changes sign where gravitational and centrifugal accelerations balance, so \(r=R_G\).
Integrating to \(R_G\) gives \[\sigma_{max}=\rho gR^2\left[\frac1R-\frac3{2R_G}+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}\right].\] For steel this is about 383 GPa, or 76.5 times its strength.
Expand each exponential to second order. Linear terms cancel and \(V=-V_0+4V_0x^2/a^2\), so \(P=-V_0\), \(Q=4V_0/a^2\).

The circumference has 27 parallel-bond spacings, so \(d=27b/\pi\). Using effective solid area \(A=\pi d^2/4\), one axial chain contributes \(ka/A\) to the modulus. For 27 parallel chains, \[E=27\frac{ka}{A}\simeq342\,\mathrm{GPa}.\] This is the source's effective solid-cylinder convention. A shell-wall-area convention would give a different quoted modulus.
The maximum strain is \(x_{max}/a=1/2\). Thus \(\sigma_0=E/2=171\,\mathrm{GPa}\). This extrapolation of the harmonic approximation is the estimate requested, not a measured strength.
An axial repeat length \(3a/2\) contains \(2\times27\) atoms. Divide their mass by \((\pi d^2/4)(3a/2)\), giving \(\rho\simeq1440\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\).

Force balance now reads \(\sigma\,dA/dr=\rho A GM(1/r^2-r/R_G^3)\). Integration gives \[A(h)=A_S\exp\left\{\frac{\rho gR^2}{\sigma}\left[\frac1R+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}-\frac1{R+h}-\frac{(R+h)^2}{2R_G^3}\right]\right\}.\]
The exponential in 3.1 must return to zero. This gives the same nontrivial root as 1.1: \[H=\frac R2[\sqrt{1+8(R_G/R)^3}-1]\simeq151000\,\mathrm{km}.\]
The maximum area is at \(R_G\). Substitute h equal to \(R_G-R\) in 3.1: \[\frac{A_G}{A_S}=\exp\left[\frac{\rho gR^2}{\sigma}\left(\frac1R-\frac3{2R_G}+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}\right)\right]\simeq1.623.\]

Let \(r_C=R_G+h_C\). The counterweight is pulled down by both gravity and cable tension: \(m_C\omega^2r_C=GMm_C/r_C^2+\sigma A(r_C-R)\). Thus \[m_C=\frac{\sigma A(r_C-R)}{\omega^2r_C-GM/r_C^2},\qquad h_C>0.\] Insert A from 3.1 for an explicit function of h_C. A counterweight at or below GEO cannot supply the required positive upward effective force.
The inertial release speed is \(\omega r\). Set \(\omega^2r^2/2-GM/r=0\) to find \[r_C=(2GM/\omega^2)^{1/3}=2^{1/3}R_G\simeq53200\,\mathrm{km}.\]

Release adds or subtracts \(v_t=\omega r_t=7.78\,\mathrm{km/s}\) to Earth's given orbital speed. For tangential heliocentric speed \(v=v_E\pm v_t\), energy and angular momentum give the other turning radius \[r_2=\frac{v^2R_E^2}{2GM_S-v^2R_E}.\] Prograde release maximizes aphelion, about 5.3 AU. Retrograde release minimizes perihelion, about 0.43 AU. The source's solar-distance estimates retain the supplied \(v_E=30.9\,\mathrm{km/s}\), even though that is not exactly the circular speed from its rounded \(M_S,R_E\).
